claim: Tissue-resident macrophages acquire diverse functions by polarizing toward distinct subpopulations.
source: Tissue-resident macrophages represent a group of highly responsive innate immune cells that acquire diverse functions by polarizing toward distinct subpopulations.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the subsequent findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The subpopulations of macrophages that reside in skeletal muscle (SKM) and their changes during aging are poorly characterized.
source: The subpopulations of macrophages that reside in skeletal muscle (SKM) and their changes during aging are poorly characterized.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis with unsupervised clustering identified 11 distinct macrophage clusters in male mouse SKM.
source: By single-cell transcriptomic analysis with unsupervised clustering, we found 11 distinct macrophage clusters in male mouse SKM with enriched gene expression programs linked to reparative, proinflammatory, phagocytic, proliferative, and senescence-associated functions.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the scRNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 1C and described in the Results section.

claim: The 11 macrophage clusters have enriched gene expression programs linked to reparative, proinflammatory, phagocytic, proliferative, and senescence-associated functions.
source: By single-cell transcriptomic analysis with unsupervised clustering, we found 11 distinct macrophage clusters in male mouse SKM with enriched gene expression programs linked to reparative, proinflammatory, phagocytic, proliferative, and senescence-associated functions.
evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis and gene expression patterns shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

claim: Membrane markers LYVE1 and MHCII identified four macrophage subgroups: LYVE1−/MHCIIhi (M1-like, classically activated), LYVE1+/MHCIIlo (M2-like, alternatively activated), LYVE1+/MHCIIhi, and LYVE1−/MHCIIlo.
source: Using a complementary classification, membrane markers LYVE1 and MHCII identified four macrophage subgroups: LYVE1−/MHCIIhi (M1-like, classically activated), LYVE1+/MHCIIlo (M2-like, alternatively activated), and two new subgroups, LYVE1+/MHCIIhi and LYVE1−/MHCIIlo.
evidence: This classification is supported by scRNA-seq analysis (Figure 3) and validated by flow cytometry (Figure 4).

claim: LYVE1+/MHCIIhi macrophages have traits of both M2 and M1 macrophages.
source: Notably, one new subgroup, LYVE1+/MHCIIhi, had traits of both M2 and M1 macrophages, while the other new subgroup, LYVE1−/MHCIIlo, displayed strong phagocytic capacity.
evidence: This is supported by GO annotation showing both M2-like and M1-like functional associations (Figure 3C).

claim: LYVE1−/MHCIIlo macrophages display strong phagocytic capacity.
source: Notably, one new subgroup, LYVE1+/MHCIIhi, had traits of both M2 and M1 macrophages, while the other new subgroup, LYVE1−/MHCIIlo, displayed strong phagocytic capacity.
evidence: This is supported by phagocytosis assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: Flow cytometric analysis validated the presence of the four macrophage subgroups in SKM.
source: Flow cytometric analysis validated the presence of the four macrophage subgroups in SKM and found that LYVE1− macrophages were more abundant than LYVE1+ macrophages in old SKM.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4A showing flow cytometry data.

claim: LYVE1− macrophages were more abundant than LYVE1+ macrophages in old SKM.
source: Flow cytometric analysis validated the presence of the four macrophage subgroups in SKM and found that LYVE1− macrophages were more abundant than LYVE1+ macrophages in old SKM.
evidence: This is supported by both scRNA-seq (Figure 7A) and flow cytometry (Figure 7B) data comparing young and old mice.

claim: Proinflammatory markers (S100a8 and S100a9 mRNAs) showed a striking increase in macrophage clusters from older mice.
source: A striking increase in proinflammatory markers (S100a8 and S100a9 mRNAs) and senescence-related markers (Gpnmb and Spp1 mRNAs) was evident in macrophage clusters from older mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7D showing differential gene expression between young and old macrophages.

claim: Senescence-related markers (Gpnmb and Spp1 mRNAs) showed a striking increase in macrophage clusters from older mice.
source: A striking increase in proinflammatory markers (S100a8 and S100a9 mRNAs) and senescence-related markers (Gpnmb and Spp1 mRNAs) was evident in macrophage clusters from older mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figures 6 and 7D showing differential gene expression between young and old macrophages.

claim: Specific macrophage subpopulations contribute to the proinflammatory and senescent traits of old SKM.
source: In sum, we have identified dynamically polarized SKM macrophages and propose that specific macrophage subpopulations contribute to the proinflammatory and senescent traits of old SKM.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential gene expression patterns observed in aged macrophages.

claim: Macrophages are heterogeneous innate immune cells.
source: Macrophages are heterogeneous innate immune cells (Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018) that provide the first line of defense against pathogens, but are also deeply involved in inflammation, dead cell removal, wound healing, and tissue remodeling (Mills et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2021; Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages provide the first line of defense against pathogens.
source: Macrophages are heterogeneous innate immune cells (Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018) that provide the first line of defense against pathogens, but are also deeply involved in inflammation, dead cell removal, wound healing, and tissue remodeling (Mills et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2021; Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages are deeply involved in inflammation, dead cell removal, wound healing, and tissue remodeling.
source: Macrophages are heterogeneous innate immune cells (Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018) that provide the first line of defense against pathogens, but are also deeply involved in inflammation, dead cell removal, wound healing, and tissue remodeling (Mills et al., 2014; Ross et al., 2021; Shapouri-Moghaddam et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages adapt to individual tissues and acquire specific tissue-dependent functions.
source: Macrophages adapt to individual tissues and acquire specific tissue-dependent functions (Wynn et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Upon transplantation, tissue-resident macrophages quickly lose their original gene expression patterns and gain host organ markers.
source: Upon transplantation, tissue-resident macrophages quickly lose their original gene expression patterns and gain host organ markers (Lavin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The tissue environment contributes to determining the tissue-specific protein production by macrophages and thereby establishes tissue-dependent expression patterns and functions.
source: The tissue environment contributes to determining the tissue-specific protein production by macrophages and thereby establishes tissue-dependent expression patterns and functions (Gautier et al., 2012; Lavin et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of macrophages should be studied in the context of their tissue of residence.
source: Hence, the function of macrophages should be studied in the context of their tissue of residence.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous statements about tissue-specific macrophage functions.

claim: Macrophages play diverse functions in tissues by differentiating into specific functional subgroups, a process usually defined as macrophage polarization.
source: Macrophages play diverse functions in tissues by differentiating into specific functional subgroups, a process usually defined as macrophage polarization (Yao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Most macrophages are known to polarize to proinflammatory M1 or anti-inflammatory M2 subgroups.
source: Most macrophages are known to polarize to proinflammatory M1 or anti-inflammatory M2 subgroups (Martinez et al., 2008; Mills et al., 2000; Rath et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages appear to be more functionally heterogeneous than simply M1 or M2.
source: While such dichotomy largely explains the strikingly different actions of macrophages commonly seen in many tissues, macrophages appear to be more functionally heterogeneous than simply M1 or M2.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent discussion of recent studies identifying additional macrophage subgroups.

claim: Recent flow cytometry and single-cell studies have identified several new macrophage subgroups in arteries, lung interstitium, heart, adipose tissue, and other tissues and organs.
source: In this regard, recent flow cytometry and single-cell studies have identified several new macrophage subgroups in arteries, lung interstitium, heart, adipose tissue, and other tissues and organs (Chakarov et al., 2019; Dick et al., 2022; Jaitin et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2018; Schyns et al., 2019) with distinct tissue-dependent polarization status.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dissecting polarization in each tissue is critical to elucidating shared and tissue-specific macrophage functions.
source: Dissecting polarization in each tissue is thus critical to elucidating shared and tissue-specific macrophage functions.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the previous statements about tissue-specific macrophage heterogeneity.

claim: Skeletal muscle (SKM) contains large numbers of macrophages that play critical roles in injury repair and regeneration.
source: Skeletal muscle (SKM) contains large numbers of macrophages that play critical roles in injury repair and regeneration (Arnold et al., 2007; Tidball, 2011; Tidball, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Macrophages assume different polarization to play distinct functions at different stages of repair after injury.
source: Macrophages assume different polarization to play distinct functions at different stages of repair after injury (Scala et al., 2021; Yang and Hu, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the absence of injury or infection, most macrophages residing in human and mouse SKM were shown to be MRC1 (CD206)+, M2-like macrophages.
source: In the absence of injury or infection, most macrophages residing in human and mouse SKM were shown to be MRC1 (CD206)+, M2-like macrophages (Cui et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The full range of macrophage subgroups and their age-related changes in SKM is poorly understood.
source: However, the full range of macrophage subgroups and their age-related changes in SKM is poorly understood (Cui and Ferrucci, 2020).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap supported by a citation.

claim: CD11b+ cells clearly separated from the rest of the mononuclear cell population.
source: As we found previously, CD11b+ cells clearly separated from the rest of the mononuclear cell population (Krasniewski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: >80% of cells expressing Cd11b mRNA were also positive for F4/80 mRNA (Adgre1 mRNA).
source: Sequencing analysis showed that >80% of cells expressing Cd11b mRNA were also positive for F4/80 mRNA (Adgre1 mRNA), another common marker for mouse macrophages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cells expressing both Cd11b mRNA and Adgre1 mRNA were considered SKM macrophages.
source: Those cells expressing both Cd11b mRNA and Adgre1 mRNA were considered SKM macrophages.
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the study.

claim: Very few cells were positive for Ly6g mRNA or Siglecf mRNA, indicating minimal contamination from neutrophils and eosinophils in the macrophage population.
source: Very few cells were positive for Ly6g mRNA or Siglecf mRNA (specific markers for neutrophils and eosinophils, respectively; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), indicating minimal contamination from these cells in our macrophage population.
evidence: This is supported by the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The distribution of macrophages across the 11 clusters was comparable among the biological replicates.
source: Overall, the distribution of macrophages across the 11 clusters was comparable among the biological replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), and the patterns of transcriptomes were also comparable among the replicates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Each cluster showed a distinct gene expression pattern.
source: Each cluster showed a distinct gene expression pattern (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the dot plot in Figure 1D showing differential gene expression across clusters.

claim: All clusters shared functional terms general to macrophages, including 'immune system process,' 'defense response,' 'response to stress,' 'cell migration,' and 'cell death.'
source: Although all clusters shared functional terms general to macrophages, including 'immune system process,' 'defense response,' 'response to stress,' 'cell migration,' and 'cell death,' each cluster also displayed distinct functional associations (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on GO enrichment analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Cluster 0 (Cl0) showed a more reparative function, with high expression of M2-type genes.
source: The largest cluster, Cl0, showed a more reparative function, with high expression of M2-type genes (Mrc1, Cd163, Lyve1, and Folr2 mRNAs) and reduced proinflammatory function compared to the other clusters (Figure 1E and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and GO analysis in Table 1.

claim: Cluster 1 (Cl1) showed a similar expression pattern as Cl0, including the expression of M2-type mRNAs, but the expression levels of these mRNAs were lower in Cl1 than in Cl0.
source: The second largest cluster, Cl1, showed a similar expression pattern as Cl0 (Figure 1D), including the expression of M2-type mRNAs (Lyve1 and Folr2 mRNAs), but the expression levels of these mRNAs were lower in Cl1 than in Cl0 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression comparisons shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: When Cl0 was excluded from the comparison, Cl1 showed strong enrichment of M2-type mRNAs and strong association with reparative functions.
source: When we excluded Cl0 and compared Cl1 with Cl2-10 (Supplementary file 1, 'Cl1 vs Cl2-10'), Cl1 showed strong enrichment of M2-type mRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and strong association with reparative functions (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and Table 1.

claim: The two largest clusters, Cl0 and Cl1, account for nearly one-half of total macrophages and displayed M2-like gene expression patterns.
source: Thus, the two largest clusters, Cl0 and Cl1, account for nearly one-half of total macrophages and displayed M2-like gene expression patterns.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the cluster sizes shown in Figure 1C and the gene expression patterns described.

claim: Clusters Cl2-9 showed very low expression of M2 marker genes and displayed more diverse functional associations.
source: Clusters Cl2-9 showed very low expression of M2 marker genes (Table 1) and instead displayed more diverse functional associations.
evidence: This is based on the GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Cl2 expressed mRNAs related to inflammation and to the functions of antigen processing and presentation.
source: Cl2 expressed mRNAs related to inflammation and to the functions of antigen processing and presentation (Figure 1E and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and GO analysis in Table 1.

claim: The mRNAs present in Cl3 were associated with cellular detoxification.
source: The mRNAs present in Cl3 were associated with cellular detoxification, and Cl4 was associated with phagocytosis and expressed elevated MHC class I (MHCI) mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Cl4 was associated with phagocytosis and expressed elevated MHC class I (MHCI) mRNAs.
source: The mRNAs present in Cl3 were associated with cellular detoxification, and Cl4 was associated with phagocytosis and expressed elevated MHC class I (MHCI) mRNAs.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Cl5 expressed mRNAs strongly associated with the inflammatory response.
source: Cl5 expressed mRNAs strongly associated with the inflammatory response.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Cl6 was enriched in mRNAs encoding proteins involved in the response to lipoprotein particles, ATP metabolism, and lipid transport.
source: Cl6 was enriched in mRNAs encoding proteins involved in the response to lipoprotein particles, ATP metabolism, and lipid transport; this cluster also expressed Gpnmb, Spp1, Ctsd, Trem2, and Gdf15 mRNAs, encoding proteins involved in senescence and aging (Henjum et al., 2016; Pazolli et al., 2009; Suda et al., 2021; Suda et al., 2022; Tanaka et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2022), and Fabp5 and Fabp4 mRNAs, encoding proteins implicated in atherosclerosis (Babaev et al., 2011; Furuhashi et al., 2007; Makowski et al., 2001; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1 and gene expression data in Figure 1E, supported by citations.

claim: Cl6 expressed Gpnmb, Spp1, Ctsd, Trem2, and Gdf15 mRNAs, encoding proteins involved in senescence and aging.
source: Cl6 was enriched in mRNAs encoding proteins involved in the response to lipoprotein particles, ATP metabolism, and lipid transport; this cluster also expressed Gpnmb, Spp1, Ctsd, Trem2, and Gdf15 mRNAs, encoding proteins involved in senescence and aging (Henjum et al., 2016; Pazolli et al., 2009; Suda et al., 2021; Suda et al., 2022; Tanaka et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2022), and Fabp5 and Fabp4 mRNAs, encoding proteins implicated in atherosclerosis (Babaev et al., 2011; Furuhashi et al., 2007; Makowski et al., 2001; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and citations to previous literature.

claim: Cl6 expressed Fabp5 and Fabp4 mRNAs, encoding proteins implicated in atherosclerosis.
source: Cl6 was enriched in mRNAs encoding proteins involved in the response to lipoprotein particles, ATP metabolism, and lipid transport; this cluster also expressed Gpnmb, Spp1, Ctsd, Trem2, and Gdf15 mRNAs, encoding proteins involved in senescence and aging (Henjum et al., 2016; Pazolli et al., 2009; Suda et al., 2021; Suda et al., 2022; Tanaka et al., 2018; Williams et al., 2022), and Fabp5 and Fabp4 mRNAs, encoding proteins implicated in atherosclerosis (Babaev et al., 2011; Furuhashi et al., 2007; Makowski et al., 2001; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and citations to previous literature.

claim: The mRNAs expressed in Cl7 were strongly associated with translation and antigen processing and presentation via MHC class II.
source: The mRNAs expressed in Cl7 were strongly associated with translation and antigen processing and presentation via MHC class II, while those expressed in Cl8 were associated with cell death and phagocytosis, although M2-type markers and MHCII genes were reduced.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The mRNAs expressed in Cl8 were associated with cell death and phagocytosis, although M2-type markers and MHCII genes were reduced.
source: The mRNAs expressed in Cl7 were strongly associated with translation and antigen processing and presentation via MHC class II, while those expressed in Cl8 were associated with cell death and phagocytosis, although M2-type markers and MHCII genes were reduced.
evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: S100a8 and S100a9 mRNAs, the most robustly elevated mRNAs in Cl8, encode proinflammatory proteins.
source: Of note, S100a8 and S100a9 mRNAs, the most robustly elevated mRNAs in Cl8, encode proinflammatory proteins (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 1E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Cl9 expressed cell cycle-related mRNAs, with elevated Top2a, Mki67, and Cdk1 mRNAs, likely representing a group of proliferating macrophages.
source: Cl9 expressed cell cycle-related mRNAs, with elevated Top2a, Mki67, and Cdk1 mRNAs (Supplementary file 1), likely representing a group of reported proliferating macrophages (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data in Supplementary file 1 and supported by a citation.

claim: Cl10 (0.5% of total CD11b+/F4/80+ macrophages) was associated with a reparative function, and one-half of Cl10 cells expressed Ly6c1 mRNA.
source: The smallest cluster, Cl10 (0.5% of total CD11b+/F4/80+macrophages [Figure 1C]) was associated with a reparative function, and one-half of Cl10 cells expressed Ly6c1 mRNA (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is based on GO analysis in Table 1 and gene expression data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Unsupervised clustering revealed a wide functional heterogeneity of SKM macrophages.
source: Overall, unsupervised clustering revealed a wide functional heterogeneity of SKM macrophages.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the diverse functional associations identified across the 11 clusters.

claim: Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs were broadly expressed in ~80% of macrophages.
source: However, our scRNA-seq data showed that Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs were broadly expressed in ~80% of macrophages, Cd80 mRNA was expressed only in a small population, and most macrophages expressed Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting they are not ideal to classify SKM macrophages at the transcriptomic level.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cd80 mRNA was expressed only in a small population of macrophages.
source: However, our scRNA-seq data showed that Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs were broadly expressed in ~80% of macrophages, Cd80 mRNA was expressed only in a small population, and most macrophages expressed Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting they are not ideal to classify SKM macrophages at the transcriptomic level.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Most macrophages expressed Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs simultaneously.
source: However, our scRNA-seq data showed that Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs were broadly expressed in ~80% of macrophages, Cd80 mRNA was expressed only in a small population, and most macrophages expressed Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting they are not ideal to classify SKM macrophages at the transcriptomic level.
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mrc1, Cd86, and Cd80 are not ideal to classify SKM macrophages at the transcriptomic level.
source: However, our scRNA-seq data showed that Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs were broadly expressed in ~80% of macrophages, Cd80 mRNA was expressed only in a small population, and most macrophages expressed Mrc1 and Cd86 mRNAs simultaneously (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), suggesting they are not ideal to classify SKM macrophages at the transcriptomic level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: LYVE1 and MHCII were successfully used to subgroup several tissue-resident macrophages.
source: Recently, LYVE1 and MHCII were successfully used to subgroup several tissue-resident macrophages (Dick et al., 2022; Chakarov et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: LYVE1 status divided SKM macrophages into two large, similarly sized groups, LYVE1+ (46.6%) and LYVE1− (53.4%).
source: LYVE1 status divided SKM macrophages into two large, similarly sized groups, LYVE1+ (46.6%) and LYVE1− (53.4%) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: LYVE1+ macrophages displayed an M2-like transcriptomic program, including mRNAs encoding proteins associated with functions in 'vasculature development,' 'wound repair,' and 'endocytosis.'
source: LYVE1+ macrophages displayed an M2-like transcriptomic program, including mRNAs encoding proteins associated with functions in 'vasculature development,' 'wound repair,' and 'endocytosis' (Figure 2B; Buchacher et al., 2015; Stein et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data in Figure 2B and citations to previous literature.

claim: Transcripts encoding proangiogenic proteins (Ang, Stab1, and Egr1 mRNAs) were upregulated in LYVE1+ macrophages.
source: Interestingly, transcripts encoding proangiogenic proteins (Ang, Stab1, and Egr1 mRNAs) as well as transcripts encoding antiangiogenic proteins (Cfh and Hspb1 mRNAs) were upregulated in LYVE1+ macrophages.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transcripts encoding antiangiogenic proteins (Cfh and Hspb1 mRNAs) were upregulated in LYVE1+ macrophages.
source: Interestingly, transcripts encoding proangiogenic proteins (Ang, Stab1, and Egr1 mRNAs) as well as transcripts encoding antiangiogenic proteins (Cfh and Hspb1 mRNAs) were upregulated in LYVE1+ macrophages.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transcripts encoding proteins implicated in wound healing (Igf1, Nrp1, and Gas6 mRNAs) were elevated in LYVE1+ macrophages.
source: Transcripts encoding proteins implicated in wound healing (Igf1, Nrp1, and Gas6 mRNAs) were also elevated in LYVE1+ macrophages (Figure 2B);
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: mRNAs encoding endocytosis-related members of the CD209 family (including Cd209d and Cd209b mRNAs) as well as Cd36, Cd163, and Mrc1 mRNAs were highly expressed in LYVE1+ macrophages.
source: and mRNAs encoding endocytosis-related members of the CD209 family (including Cd209d and Cd209b mRNAs) as well as Cd36, Cd163, and Mrc1 mRNAs were also highly expressed in LYVE1+ macrophages.
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Timd4 and Fcna mRNAs were almost exclusively expressed in the LYVE1+ macrophages and might be good candidate markers for this population.
source: Other mRNAs, such as Timd4 and Fcna mRNAs, were almost exclusively expressed in the LYVE1+ macrophages and might be good candidate markers for this population (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding antigen-processing and antigen-presenting proteins (H2-Eb1, H2-Ab1, H2-DMb1, and Cd74 mRNAs).
source: In contrast, LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding antigen-processing and antigen-presenting proteins (H2-Eb1, H2-Ab1, H2-DMb1, and Cd74 mRNAs), proteins related to the NF-kB signaling pathway and implicated in cell death (Il1b, Bcl2a1b, Bcl2a1d, Cd14, Traf1, and Malt1 mRNAs), and proteins with function in antioxidant responses (Gsr, Prdx5, Prdx6, Prdx1, and Hp mRNAs).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding proteins related to the NF-kB signaling pathway and implicated in cell death (Il1b, Bcl2a1b, Bcl2a1d, Cd14, Traf1, and Malt1 mRNAs).
source: In contrast, LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding antigen-processing and antigen-presenting proteins (H2-Eb1, H2-Ab1, H2-DMb1, and Cd74 mRNAs), proteins related to the NF-kB signaling pathway and implicated in cell death (Il1b, Bcl2a1b, Bcl2a1d, Cd14, Traf1, and Malt1 mRNAs), and proteins with function in antioxidant responses (Gsr, Prdx5, Prdx6, Prdx1, and Hp mRNAs).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding proteins with function in antioxidant responses (Gsr, Prdx5, Prdx6, Prdx1, and Hp mRNAs).
source: In contrast, LYVE1− macrophages expressed higher levels of mRNAs encoding antigen-processing and antigen-presenting proteins (H2-Eb1, H2-Ab1, H2-DMb1, and Cd74 mRNAs), proteins related to the NF-kB signaling pathway and implicated in cell death (Il1b, Bcl2a1b, Bcl2a1d, Cd14, Traf1, and Malt1 mRNAs), and proteins with function in antioxidant responses (Gsr, Prdx5, Prdx6, Prdx1, and Hp mRNAs).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Many mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins were highly expressed in LYVE1− macrophages.
source: In addition, many mRNAs encoding ribosomal proteins were highly expressed in this group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on gene expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RT-qPCR analysis confirmed that Lyve1, Folr2, Timd4, CD209f, and Fcna mRNAs were almost exclusively expressed in LYVE1+ macrophages.
source: Reverse transcription (RT) followed by real-time quantitative (q)PCR analysis confirmed that Lyve1, Folr2, Timd4, CD209f, and Fcna mRNAs were almost exclusively expressed in LYVE1 + macrophages (Figure 2D, top, n=2 biological replicates).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Mrc1, Igf1, and Ang mRNAs were expressed in both LYVE1+ and LYVE1− macrophages, but at much higher levels in LYVE1+.
source: By contrast, Mrc1, Igf1, and Ang mRNAs were expressed in both LYVE1+ and LYVE1− macrophages, but at much higher levels in LYVE1+, while Il1b mRNA levels were significantly higher in the LYVE1− population (Figure 2D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Il1b mRNA levels were significantly higher in the LYVE1− population.
source: By contrast, Mrc1, Igf1, and Ang mRNAs were expressed in both LYVE1+ and LYVE1− macrophages, but at much higher levels in LYVE1+, while Il1b mRNA levels were significantly higher in the LYVE1− population (Figure 2D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The RT-qPCR results were consistent with the single-cell transcriptomic analysis, indicating that LYVE1 is an effective marker for subgrouping mouse SKM macrophages.
source: The RT-qPCR results (Figure 2D) were consistent with the single-cell transcriptomic analysis (Figure 2B and C; Supplementary file 2), indicating that LYVE1 is an effective marker for subgrouping mouse SKM macrophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistency between RT-qPCR and scRNA-seq data.

claim: The membrane marker MHCII (encoded by H2-Ab1 and H2-Eb1 mRNAs) divided SKM macrophages into two groups, MHCIIhi and MHCIIlo.
source: By single-cell profiling analysis, the membrane marker MHCII (encoded by H2-Ab1 and H2-Eb1 mRNAs) divided SKM macrophages into two groups, MHCIIhi and MHCIIlo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Considering the relative levels of LYVE1 and MHCII on the membrane allowed the classification of SKM macrophages into four subgroups: LYVE1+/MHCIIhi, LYVE1+/MHCIIlo, LYVE1−/MHCIIhi, and LYVE1−/MHCIIlo.
source: Considering the relative levels of LYVE1 and MHCII on the membrane allowed the classification of SKM macrophages into four subgroups: LYVE1+/MHCIIhi, LYVE1+/MHCIIlo, LYVE1−/MHCIIhi, and LYVE1−/MHCIIlo (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LYVE1+/MHCIIhi and LYVE1−/MHCIIhi were the largest subgroups, comprising 36.55 and 39.97% of all macrophages, respectively.
source: Among them, LYVE1+/MHCIIhi and LYVE1−/MHCIIhi were the largest subgroups, comprising 36.55 and 39.97% of all macrophages, respectively (Figure 3A), while LYVE1+/MHCIIlo and LYVE1−/MHCIIlo comprised 10.09 and 13.39%, respectively (biological replicates in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, C).
